title: Hosea

stories.title: 💔 Hosea 1
summaryBullets: This is the word of the LORD that came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and of Jeroboam son of Jehoash, king of Israel. (1:1).

When the LORD first spoke through Hosea, He told him, “Go, take a prostitute as your wife and have children of adultery, because this land is flagrantly prostituting itself by departing from the LORD.” (1:2).
So Hosea went and married Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son. (1:3).
Then the LORD said to Hosea, “Name him Jezreel, for soon I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will put an end to the kingdom of Israel. (1:4).
And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel.” (1:5).

Gomer again conceived and gave birth to a daughter, and the LORD said to Hosea, “Name her Lo-ruhamah, for I will no longer have compassion on the house of Israel, that I should ever forgive them. (1:6).
Yet I will have compassion on the house of Judah, and I will save them — not by bow or sword or war, not by horses and cavalry, but by the LORD their God.” (1:7).
After she had weaned Lo-ruhamah, Gomer conceived and gave birth to a son. (1:8).
And the LORD said, “Name him Lo-ammi, for you are not My people, and I am not your God. (1:9).

Yet the number of the Israelites will be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted. And it will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’ (1:10).
Then the people of Judah and of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint for themselves one leader, and will go up out of the land. For great will be the day of Jezreel. (1:11).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 9:30-37: Jehu has Jezebel thrown from the window at Jezreel, the bloodshed charged against his house.
2 Kings 14:23-29: Jeroboam son of Jehoash reigns forty-one years in Samaria, the king named in the opening verse.
2 Kings 17:5-6: Assyria besieges Samaria three years, takes it, and deports Israel to Halah and Gozan and the cities of the Medes.
Genesis 22:17: The promise to Abraham that his offspring will be as the sand on the seashore.
Romans 9:25-26: Paul quotes these very names, Not My People and sons of the living God, in Romans.

translationNotes.note: 1:1 dates the book by five reigns. Jeroboam son of Joash ruled the northern kingdom for about forty years and 2 Kings 14:25-28 credits him with recovering territory from Lebanon to the Dead Sea, so Hosea begins preaching in a boom. The four Judean kings that follow carry the list down past his death, through the years the northern kingdom went through five kings in ten years and fell to Assyria in 722 BC.

Zenunim is the plural abstract of the verb to prostitute, and 1:2 uses it twice in one sentence, for the wife and for the land. The book runs on that one figure because the covenant at Sinai is framed as a marriage, so serving another god is not an error of judgement but a wife taking money from other men. Hosea is told to live it in public.

Jezreel is both a city and the broad valley that cuts the country in half between Galilee and Samaria, flat, watered, and the ground armies fought over for centuries. It is where Jehu killed Joram, Jezebel and the whole house of Ahab and had seventy heads of Ahab's sons piled at the gate (2 Kings 9-10). 1:4 names the child for that bloodshed, and 1:5 breaks Israel's bow in the same valley.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא רֻחָמָה (Lo Ruchamah, not pitied) - לֹא עַמִּי (Lo Ammi, not my people)
translationNotes.note: Both names, given at 1:6 and 1:9, are sentences with the word not fixed to the front, so the children carried a verdict around with them every time they were called. Racham, behind Ruhamah, is built on rechem, the womb, and it is the compassion a mother has for the child she carried. 2:23 reverses both names, and Paul quotes that reversal at Romans 9:25-26.

translationNotes.term: I am not ehyeh to you
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְאָנֹכִי לֹא־אֶהְיֶה לָכֶם (ve-anokhi lo ehyeh lakhem)
translationNotes.note: The second half of 1:9 is usually rendered I am not your God, and the Hebrew word there is ehyeh, I will be. That is the name given to Moses at the bush in Exodus 3:14, ehyeh asher ehyeh. English hides it, but the sentence takes the covenant formula, I will be your God and you will be my people (Exodus 6:7), and cancels both halves using the name itself.

The command in 1:2 carries its own reason in the same sentence, because the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD. The three children are given names that are messages, and the text explains each one on the spot at 1:4-9, then reverses all three inside the book: Not My People becomes sons of the living God at 1:10, and both No Compassion and Not My People are undone at 2:23. The second command, at 3:1, is worded the same way.

stories.keyTakeaway: God commands Hosea to marry Gomer, a promiscuous woman, and their three children receive names signifying Israel's unfaithfulness and coming judgment; yet God promises eventual restoration for both Israel and Judah.

stories.title: 💔 Hosea 2
summaryBullets: “Say of your brothers, ‘My people,’ and of your sisters, ‘My loved one.’ (2:1).
Rebuke your mother, rebuke her, for she is not My wife, and I am not her husband. Let her remove the adultery from her face and the unfaithfulness from between her breasts. (2:2).
Otherwise, I will strip her naked and expose her like the day of her birth. I will make her like a desert and turn her into a parched land, and I will let her die of thirst. (2:3).
I will have no compassion on her children, because they are the children of adultery. (2:4).
For their mother has played the harlot and has conceived them in disgrace. For she thought, ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me bread and water, wool and linen, oil and drink.’ (2:5).
Therefore, behold, I will hedge up her path with thorns; I will enclose her with a wall, so she cannot find her way. (2:6).
She will pursue her lovers but not catch them; she will seek them but not find them. Then she will say, ‘I will return to my first husband, for then I was better off than now.’ (2:7).
For she does not acknowledge that it was I who gave her grain, new wine, and oil, who lavished on her silver and gold — which they crafted for Baal. (2:8).
Therefore I will take back My grain in its time and My new wine in its season; I will take away My wool and linen, which were given to cover her nakedness. (2:9).
And then I will expose her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and no one will deliver her out of My hands. (2:10).
I will put an end to all her exultation: her feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths— all her appointed feasts. (2:11).
I will destroy her vines and fig trees, which she thinks are the wages paid by her lovers. So I will make them into a thicket, and the beasts of the field will devour them. (2:12).
I will punish her for the days of the Baals when she burned incense to them, when she adorned herself with rings and jewelry, and went after her lovers. But Me she forgot,” declares the LORD. (2:13).
“Therefore, behold, I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly. (2:14).
There I will give back her vineyards and make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope. There she will respond as she did in the days of her youth, as in the day she came up out of Egypt. (2:15).
In that day,” declares the LORD, “you will call Me ‘my Husband,’ and no longer call Me ‘my Master.’ (2:16).
For I will remove from her lips the names of the Baals; no longer will their names be invoked. (2:17).

On that day I will make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field and the birds of the air and the creatures that crawl on the ground. And I will abolish bow and sword and battle in the land, and will make them lie down in safety. (2:18).
So I will betroth you to Me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion. (2:19).
And I will betroth you in faithfulness, and you will know the LORD.” (2:20).
“On that day I will respond —” declares the LORD — “I will respond to the heavens, and they will respond to the earth. (2:21).
And the earth will respond to the grain, to the new wine and oil, and they will respond to Jezreel. (2:22).
And I will sow her as My own in the land, and I will have compassion on ‘No Compassion.’ I will say to those called ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are My people,’ and they will say, ‘You are my God.’” (2:23).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 18:20-40: Elijah faces the prophets of Baal on Carmel, and they call on him from morning until noon with no answer.
Deuteronomy 11:13-17: The LORD is the one who gives the autumn and spring rains, the grain, the new wine and the oil.
Numbers 28:11-15: The New Moon offering, one of the appointed times Hosea says will be brought to an end.
Joshua 7:24-26: Achan is judged in the Valley of Achor, which carries the name Trouble from that day.
Deuteronomy 22:23-24: Betrothal is legally binding, so a betrothed woman is already treated in law as a wife.

translationNotes.term: My Husband, and no longer my Master
translationNotes.note: Baal is an ordinary Hebrew noun meaning owner or master, and it is also the normal word a woman used for her husband. It is likewise the name of the Canaanite storm god who was credited with sending the rain, and so with the grain, wine, and oil in verse 8. Verse 16 turns on that collision: she will call Him ishi, my man, and stop calling Him baali, because the second word cannot be said any more without saying the god's name.

translationNotes.term: The wages paid by her lovers
translationNotes.note: Etnah is the fee paid to a prostitute. Deuteronomy 23:18 forbids bringing that money into the house of the LORD, and Micah 1:7 says Samaria's images were bought with it and will be carried off as it. The list in verse 5, bread and water, wool and linen, oil and drink, is what a husband was legally required to provide his wife (Exodus 21:10); she is calling the husband's own provision her lovers' pay.

translationNotes.term: Her feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths
translationNotes.note: Israel's calendar ran on the moon. Each month began at the new moon with trumpet blasts and set sacrifices (Numbers 10:10; 28:11-15), the sabbath fell every seventh day, and the appointed feasts of Leviticus 23 were Passover and Unleavened Bread, Weeks, Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and Tabernacles. Verse 11 is God shutting down the whole religious year at once.

Achor means trouble. Joshua 7:24-26 names the place: after Achan took plunder from Jericho that had been devoted to destruction, he and his household were taken to that valley, stoned, and buried under a heap of stones, and Joshua said, why have you troubled us, the LORD will trouble you this day. It lies in the dry country north of the Dead Sea near Jericho. Verse 15 makes the valley named for disaster into a door of hope.

translationNotes.term: I will betroth you to Me
translationNotes.note: Betrothal in Israel was not an engagement that could be called off by changing your mind. The bride price was paid and the woman was legally the man's wife from that moment, which is why Deuteronomy 22:23-24 treats unfaithfulness by a betrothed woman as adultery and why Joseph had to consider a divorce rather than a broken engagement (Matthew 1:18-19). The verb is repeated three times in verses 19 and 20.

stories.keyTakeaway: God declares through Hosea that Israel's unfaithfulness will bring punishment - stripped of provisions, blocked from her lovers, her festivals ceased - but then promises to allure her back to the wilderness, restore her vineyards, and betroth her forever in righteousness and faithfulness.

stories.title: 💔 Hosea 3
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to me, “Go show love to your wife again, though she is loved by another and is an adulteress. Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods and love to offer raisin cakes to idols.” (3:1).
So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley. (3:2).
Then I said to her, “You must live with me for many days; you must not be promiscuous or belong to another, and I will do the same for you.” (3:3).
For the Israelites must live many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or sacred pillar, and without ephod or idol. (3:4).
Afterward, the people of Israel will return and seek the LORD their God and David their king. They will come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness in the last days. (3:5).
crossRefs: Exodus 21:32: Thirty shekels of silver is the fixed payment for a slave killed by an ox, twice what Hosea pays here.
Leviticus 27:1-4: The sanctuary valuation of persons, fifty shekels for a man and thirty for a woman.
2 Samuel 6:19: David hands out a loaf, a date cake and a raisin cake to the whole crowd at the ark's return.
Exodus 28:6-14: The ephod worn by the high priest, worked in gold, blue, purple and scarlet yarn.
Ezekiel 37:24-25: My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וָאֶכְּרֶהָ לִּי (va-ekkereha li, and I bought her for myself)
translationNotes.note: 3:2 pays fifteen shekels of silver plus a homer and a lethech of barley. The verb is karah, to purchase or acquire, and it is not the ordinary word for buying goods. This is a woman already his wife being paid for a second time, out of whatever hand held her.

translationNotes.term: What the buy-back price was worth
translationNotes.note: Half the payment at 3:2 is metal and half is grain. Silver was weighed out, not counted; a shekel ran about four tenths of an ounce, roughly eleven grams, so fifteen shekels is close to six ounces of silver. Thirty shekels was the fixed compensation for a slave killed by an ox (Exodus 21:32) and the sanctuary valuation of a woman (Leviticus 27:4), so this is exactly half the standard figure. A homer is ten ephahs, a little over six bushels, and a lethech is half a homer, which puts the barley at roughly nine bushels.

Barley was the cheap grain, poor man's bread and animal feed, harvested weeks before the wheat. The law prices a barley field accordingly (Leviticus 27:16), and the jealousy offering at Numbers 5:15 is barley flour with no oil and no incense on it, the plainest offering in the system. Paying half of 3:2 in barley says what kind of transaction this was.

Pressed cakes of dried grapes, festival food handed out at public celebrations (2 Samuel 6:19). At 3:1 they are what Israel loves while turning to other gods, because the harvest feasts at the Baal shrines ran on the same food and drink. Jeremiah 7:18 shows the same pattern in Judah, whole households baking cakes for the queen of heaven.

3:4 lists what Israel will go without, and every item is a physical object. A matsevah is a standing stone erected at a shrine, which Deuteronomy 16:22 forbids outright. The ephod is the priestly vestment used to seek an answer from God (1 Samuel 23:9-12). Teraphim are household gods, the figures Rachel stole from her father (Genesis 31:19) and the one Michal put in a bed to fake a sleeping man (1 Samuel 19:13), and Ezekiel 21:21 shows them used for divination.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵין מֶלֶךְ וְאֵין שָׂר (en melekh ve-en sar)
translationNotes.note: 3:4 strips out two systems at once: the state, king and officer, and the whole apparatus of worship, sacrifice and pillar and ephod and household gods. What is left is many days of neither. 3:5 then says afterward they will seek the LORD and David their king, so the sentence is bounded and the text says so.

stories.keyTakeaway: God commands Hosea to buy back his unfaithful wife for silver and barley, requiring her to live with him in separation; the passage compares this to how Israel will eventually return to seek the LORD after a long period without king, sacrifice, or idols.

stories.title: 🧭 Hosea 4
summaryBullets: Hear the word of the LORD, O children of Israel, for the LORD has a case against the people of the land: “There is no truth, no loving devotion, and no knowledge of God in the land! (4:1).
Cursing and lying, murder and stealing, and adultery are rampant; one act of bloodshed follows another. (4:2).
Therefore the land mourns, and all who dwell in it will waste away with the beasts of the field and the birds of the air; even the fish of the sea disappear. (4:3).
But let no man contend; let no man offer reproof; for your people are like those who contend with a priest. (4:4).
You will stumble by day, and the prophet will stumble with you by night; so I will destroy your mother — (4:5).

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you as My priests. Since you have forgotten the law of your God, I will also forget your children. (4:6).
The more they multiplied, the more they sinned against Me; they exchanged their Glory for a thing of disgrace. (4:7).
They feed on the sins of My people and set their hearts on iniquity. (4:8).
And it shall be like people, like priest. I will punish both of them for their ways and repay them for their deeds. (4:9).
They will eat but not be satisfied; they will be promiscuous but not multiply. For they have abandoned the LORD to give themselves (4:10).
to promiscuity, wine, and new wine, which take away understanding. (4:11).
My people consult their wooden idols, and their divining rods inform them. For a spirit of prostitution leads them astray and they have played the harlot against their God. (4:12).

They sacrifice on the mountaintops and burn offerings on the hills, under oak, poplar, and terebinth, because their shade is pleasant. And so your daughters turn to prostitution and your daughters-in-law to adultery. (4:13).

I will not punish your daughters when they prostitute themselves, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery. For the men themselves go off with prostitutes and offer sacrifices with shrine prostitutes. So a people without understanding will come to ruin. (4:14).
Though you prostitute yourself, O Israel, may Judah avoid such guilt! Do not journey to Gilgal, do not go up to Beth-aven, and do not swear on oath, ‘As surely as the LORD lives!’ (4:15).
For Israel is as obstinate as a stubborn heifer. Can the LORD now shepherd them like lambs in an open meadow? (4:16).
Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone! (4:17).
When their liquor is gone, they turn to prostitution; their rulers dearly love disgrace. (4:18).
The whirlwind has wrapped them in its wings, and their sacrifices will bring them shame. (4:19).
crossRefs: Exodus 20:13-15: You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal.
Deuteronomy 12:2-4: Destroy every place on the high mountains and under every green tree where the nations served their gods.
Deuteronomy 23:17-18: No son or daughter of Israel is to be a shrine prostitute, and such wages may not enter the LORD's house.
Malachi 2:7-8: The lips of a priest should preserve knowledge, because he is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts.
Joshua 5:9-10: Gilgal is where the reproach of Egypt was rolled away and Israel kept the first Passover in the land.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶפְרַיִם, Greek (LXX): Ἐφραΐμ, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): אפרים
translationNotes.note: Shorthand for the Northern Kingdom/Israel (many times in Hosea).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רוּחַ זְנוּנִים, Greek (LXX): πνεῦμα πορνείας, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): רוחא דזנונין
translationNotes.note: Phrase for the driving unfaithfulness behind idol-sex (4:12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֶלֶךְ יָרֵב, Greek (LXX): βασιλεὺς Ἰαρίμ/Ἰαρείμ (var.), Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): מלכא דריבא ('war-making/contending king')
translationNotes.note: Likely a title (“great/contending king”) for Assyria rather than a personal name (5:13).

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD accuses Israel of faithlessness, murder, theft, and adultery; the land withers as a result. Because the priests reject knowledge and lead people into idolatry and prostitution, God will punish both them and their followers, and Israel will be swept away like chaff.

stories.title: 🧭 Hosea 5
summaryBullets: “Hear this, O priests! Take heed, O house of Israel! Give ear, O royal house! For this judgment is against you because you have been a snare at Mizpah, a net spread out on Tabor. (5:1).
The rebels are deep in slaughter; but I will chastise them all. (5:2).
I know all about Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from Me. For now, O Ephraim, you have turned to prostitution; Israel is defiled. (5:3).
Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God, for a spirit of prostitution is within them, and they do not know the LORD. (5:4).
Israel’s arrogance testifies against them; Israel and Ephraim stumble in their iniquity; even Judah stumbles with them. (5:5).
They go with their flocks and herds to seek the LORD, but they do not find Him; He has withdrawn Himself from them. (5:6).
They have been unfaithful to the LORD; for they have borne illegitimate children. Now the New Moon will devour them along with their land. (5:7).
Blow the ram’s horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; raise the battle cry in Beth-aven: Lead on, O Benjamin! (5:8).
Ephraim will be laid waste on the day of rebuke. Among the tribes of Israel I proclaim what is certain. (5:9).
The princes of Judah are like those who move boundary stones; I will pour out My fury upon them like water. (5:10).
Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, for he is determined to follow worthless idols. (5:11).
So I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like decay to the house of Judah. (5:12).
When Ephraim saw his sickness and Judah his wound, then Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to the great king. But he cannot cure you or heal your wound. (5:13).
For I am like a lion to Ephraim and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, even I, will tear them to pieces and then go away. I will carry them off where no one can rescue them. (5:14).
Then I will return to My place until they admit their guilt and seek My face; in their affliction they will earnestly seek Me.” (5:15).
crossRefs: Judges 4:6-14: Barak masses ten thousand men on Mount Tabor and charges down on Sisera and his nine hundred iron chariots.
Numbers 10:1-10: Two hammered silver trumpets summon the assembly and sound the alarm when the enemy attacks.
Deuteronomy 27:17: Cursed is he who moves his neighbor's boundary stone, and all the people say Amen.
2 Kings 15:19-20: Menahem pays Pul of Assyria a thousand talents of silver, exacted fifty shekels a man from the wealthy.
2 Kings 16:7-9: Ahaz calls Tiglath-pileser of Assyria his lord and empties the temple treasury to buy his help.

translationNotes.term: A snare at Mizpah, a net on Tabor
translationNotes.note: Both are high places where people gathered. Mizpah means watchtower; the one in Gilead is where Jacob and Laban piled a heap of stones and swore a pact (Genesis 31:44-49), and Mizpah in Benjamin is where Israel assembled before the LORD (Judges 20:1; 1 Samuel 7:5-6). Tabor is the isolated dome of a hill rising out of the Jezreel valley in the north, where Barak mustered ten thousand men before going down on Sisera (Judges 4:6-14). Verse 1 says the leadership turned the gathering places into traps.

translationNotes.term: The ram's horn and the trumpet
translationNotes.note: Two different instruments. A shophar is a natural horn from a ram or a wild goat, curved, blown as an alarm or a signal and audible for miles. A chatsotserah is a straight trumpet of hammered silver, and Numbers 10:1-10 orders two of them made and lays out the code: one blown to summon the leaders, both for the whole assembly, and a different pattern to break camp or to sound the alarm for war.

Three towns strung along the ridge road running north out of Jerusalem through Benjamin, listed as an invasion route. Gibeah was Saul's home town and the scene of the atrocity in Judges 19-20; Ramah was Samuel's home and circuit stop (1 Samuel 7:17). Beth-aven means house of wickedness, and it is Hosea's deliberate renaming of Bethel, house of God, where Jeroboam set up one of the two golden calves (1 Kings 12:28-29; Hosea 4:15; 10:5).

A moth eats woollen cloth quietly from the inside until the garment falls apart when you pick it up, and raqav is the rot that hollows out timber or bone. Both are slow and invisible while they work. Verse 14 then switches images entirely, from the thing you never notice to a lion that tears and carries off.

translationNotes.term: Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to the great king
translationNotes.note: Assyria was the empire on the Tigris, ruling from Asshur, Calah, and Nineveh, and its standing policy was tribute from client kings and mass deportation for any state that stopped paying. The northern kingdom did both: Hoshea paid, then stopped, and Samaria fell in 722 BC with the population carried off to Halah, the Habor, and the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:3-6). The Hebrew rendered King Jareb reads more naturally as a title, the great king or the contending king, which is exactly how Assyria's envoy announces his master at the wall of Jerusalem in 2 Kings 18:19.

stories.keyTakeaway: God announces judgment against Israel's priests and leaders for their corruption and idolatry; though they will seek him in distress, he has withdrawn from them and will tear them apart like a lion until they acknowledge their guilt.

stories.title: 🔁 Hosea 6
summaryBullets: Come, let us return to the LORD. For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us; He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds. (6:1).
After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence. (6:2).
So let us know — let us press on to know the LORD. As surely as the sun rises, He will appear; He will come to us like the rain, like the spring showers that water the earth. (6:3).
What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? For your loyalty is like a morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes. (6:4).
Therefore I have hewn them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of My mouth, and My judgments go forth like lightning. (6:5).
For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. (6:6).
But they, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant; there they were unfaithful to Me. (6:7).
Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with footprints of blood. (6:8).
Like raiders who lie in ambush, so does a band of priests; they murder on the way to Shechem; surely they have committed atrocities. (6:9).
In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing: Ephraim practices prostitution there, and Israel is defiled. (6:10).
Also for you, O Judah, a harvest is appointed, when I restore My people from captivity. (6:11).
crossRefs: Matthew 9:13: Jesus tells His critics to go and learn what I desire mercy, not sacrifice means.
Deuteronomy 32:39: I bring death and I give life, I wound and I heal, and no one can deliver from My hand.
Genesis 3:6-12: Adam eats, hides among the trees, and is called out and questioned by the LORD God.
Joshua 20:7-8: Shechem and Ramoth in Gilead are set apart as cities of refuge, the two places named here as bloodstained.
Micah 6:6-8: What the LORD requires is to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God.

translationNotes.note: Chesed is the loyalty owed inside a binding relationship, which is why translations swing between mercy, steadfast love and kindness for one word. 6:6 sets it against zevach, a slaughtered animal offering, and says God wants the first rather than the second. Jesus quotes this verse twice, at Matthew 9:13 when He eats with tax collectors and at Matthew 12:7 over the grain fields on the sabbath.

Yada, the verb behind da'ath, is knowing by experience and contact, not by information; Genesis 4:1 uses it for a husband knowing his wife. So the knowledge 6:6 asks for is not doctrine held in the head. 4:1 and 4:6 make it the charge sheet of the whole book: no knowledge of God in the land, and a people destroyed for lack of it.

The same three letters give the man Adam, the word for mankind, and the town of Adam, and 6:7 can be read as any of them. Adam is a real place: Joshua 3:16 says the Jordan's water stood in a heap as far back as the city of Adam beside Zarethan when Israel crossed. The next verses name Gilead and Shechem, which are also towns, and the app leaves the line as the text has it.

translationNotes.term: The early and the latter rain
translationNotes.note: Israel's farming year rides on two rains and 6:3 names them both. The yoreh falls in October or November and softens ground baked hard all summer so a plow can break it. The malqosh falls in March or April and fills out the grain just before harvest. Miss either and the year fails, which is why Deuteronomy 11:14 puts both in the covenant blessing.

translationNotes.term: Gilead, a city tracked with blood
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲקֻבָּה מִדָּם (aquibbah mi-dam, footprinted with blood)
translationNotes.note: Gilead is the highland east of the Jordan, and 6:8 says its streets carry bloody footprints. The Hebrew builds on aqev, a heel, so the picture is tracks left behind by men walking away from a killing. Judges 12:4-6 and 2 Kings 15:25 both record blood spilled there.

translationNotes.term: Murder on the road to Shechem
translationNotes.note: Shechem sits in the pass between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim and was a city of refuge, one of six a man who killed without intent could run to and stand trial in instead of being cut down on the road (Joshua 20:7). 6:9 has bands of priests lying in ambush on the way to it. The verb is ratsach, the verb of the sixth commandment, so the men set over the sanctuary are doing on that road exactly what the road existed to prevent.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel is called to return to the LORD, who will heal their wounds; but God responds that their love is fleeting like morning mist, their sacrifices mean nothing without mercy and acknowledgment, and he condemns them for breaking the covenant, bloodshed, priestly murder, and prostitution.

headings.text: The Unrepentance of Israel and Judah

stories.title: 🔁 Hosea 7
summaryBullets: When I heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim will be exposed, as well as the crimes of Samaria. For they practice deceit and thieves break in; bandits raid in the streets. (7:1).
But they fail to consider in their hearts that I remember all their evil. Now their deeds are all around them; they are before My face. (7:2).
They delight the king with their evil, and the princes with their lies. (7:3).
They are all adulterers, like an oven heated by a baker who needs not stoke the fire from the kneading to the rising of the dough. (7:4).
The princes are inflamed with wine on the day of our king; so he joins hands with those who mock him. (7:5).
For they prepare their heart like an oven while they lie in wait; all night their anger smolders; in the morning it blazes like a flaming fire. (7:6).
All of them are hot as an oven, and they devour their rulers. All their kings fall; not one of them calls upon Me. (7:7).
Ephraim mixes with the nations; Ephraim is an unturned cake. (7:8).
Foreigners consume his strength, but he does not notice. Even his hair is streaked with gray, but he does not know. (7:9).
Israel’s arrogance testifies against them, yet they do not return to the LORD their God; despite all this, they do not seek Him. (7:10).
So Ephraim has become like a silly, senseless dove — calling out to Egypt, then turning to Assyria. (7:11).
As they go, I will spread My net over them; I will bring them down like birds of the air. I will chastise them when I hear them flocking together. (7:12).
Woe to them, for they have strayed from Me! Destruction to them, for they have rebelled against Me! Though I would redeem them, they speak lies against Me. (7:13).
They do not cry out to Me from their hearts when they wail upon their beds. They slash themselves for grain and new wine, but turn away from Me. (7:14).
Although I trained and strengthened their arms, they plot evil against Me. (7:15).
They turn, but not to the Most High; they are like a faulty bow. Their leaders will fall by the sword for the cursing of their tongue; for this they will be ridiculed in the land of Egypt. (7:16).
crossRefs: Leviticus 2:4-5: Grain offerings baked in an oven or on a griddle, the baker's work behind the images in this chapter.
2 Kings 15:8-15: Zechariah is murdered after six months, Shallum after one, in the run of assassinations Hosea describes.
2 Kings 17:3-4: Hoshea sends envoys to So king of Egypt while paying tribute to Assyria, and Assyria jails him for it.
1 Kings 18:28: The prophets of Baal gash themselves with knives and lances until the blood runs.
Psalm 78:57: They turned back and were faithless, twisted like a faulty bow.

translationNotes.note: A tannur was a clay cylinder heated with brushwood until the walls glowed. The baker fires it, then leaves it banked while the dough rises, then stirs it up again, and 7:4-7 runs that whole cycle as one image: the fire covered overnight, blazing by morning, and the baker himself asleep. Verse 7 gives the outcome, all their kings have fallen, which is plain history; the northern kingdom went through four murdered kings in about fifteen years.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֻגָה בְּלִי הֲפוּכָה (ugah beli haphukhah)
translationNotes.note: Bread was a flat round slapped onto the hot inner wall of the oven or laid on heated stones, and it had to be flipped. Leave it and you get one side burned black and the other side raw dough, and the loaf is no use to anyone. That is what 7:8 calls Ephraim, and 7:9 carries it on: strangers eat his strength, grey hair is showing, and he has not noticed either.

translationNotes.term: Calling to Egypt, going to Assyria
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹנָה פוֹתָה אֵין לֵב (yonah photah en lev, a silly dove without sense)
translationNotes.note: 7:11 describes a foreign policy, not a mood. Hoshea, the last king of Israel, paid tribute to Assyria and at the same time sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and when Shalmaneser found out he arrested him and besieged Samaria (2 Kings 17:3-4). Playing two empires against each other is what the dove image is for: a bird flying between two nets.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶפְרוֹשׂ עֲלֵיהֶם רִשְׁתִּי (ephros alehem rishti, I will spread my net over them)
translationNotes.note: A fowler baited a patch of ground and set a net on light frames that snapped shut over the whole flock at once when he pulled the cord. Nobody escapes it by being quick, which is the force of 7:12. The same trade supplies the images at 9:8, Psalm 124:7 and Proverbs 1:17.

7:14 has them cutting themselves over grain and new wine. Self-laceration was a standard Baal rite; 1 Kings 18:28 has the prophets of Baal on Carmel cutting themselves with swords and lances until the blood ran, to make their god answer. The law forbids it by name at Leviticus 19:28 and Deuteronomy 14:1. Hosea's charge is that Israel is doing the Baal rite and expecting the LORD to send the harvest.

A composite bow was built up from wood, horn and sinew glued in layers, and damp or age separated the layers so the limbs no longer pulled true. A bow like that still looks fine and still shoots; the arrow simply goes somewhere else. 7:16 says Israel turns, but not upward, and is that bow. Psalm 78:57 uses the same phrase of the fathers in the wilderness.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hosea accuses Ephraim and Israel of pervasive deceit, adultery, and wickedness; they court foreign nations instead of seeking God, and despite God's training and desire to redeem them, they remain oblivious to their sin and will face destruction. God promises to trap them like birds and their leaders will fall by the sword.

stories.title: 🌪️ Hosea 8
summaryBullets: Put the ram’s horn to your lips! An eagle looms over the house of the LORD, because the people have transgressed My covenant and rebelled against My law. (8:1).
Israel cries out to Me, “O our God, we know You!” (8:2).
But Israel has rejected good; an enemy will pursue him. (8:3).
They set up kings, but not by Me. They make princes, but without My approval. With their silver and gold they make themselves idols, to their own destruction. (8:4).
He has rejected your calf, O Samaria. My anger burns against them. How long will they be incapable of innocence? (8:5).
For this thing is from Israel— a craftsman made it, and it is not God. It will be broken to pieces, that calf of Samaria. (8:6).
For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. There is no standing grain; what sprouts fails to yield flour. Even if it should produce, the foreigners would swallow it up. (8:7).
Israel is swallowed up! Now they are among the nations like a worthless vessel. (8:8).
For they have gone up to Assyria like a wild donkey on its own. Ephraim has hired lovers. (8:9).
Though they hire allies among the nations, I will now round them up, and they will begin to diminish under the oppression of the king of princes. (8:10).
Though Ephraim multiplied the altars for sin, they became his altars for sinning. (8:11).
Though I wrote for them the great things of My law, they regarded them as something strange. (8:12).
Though they offer sacrifices as gifts to Me, and though they eat the meat, the LORD does not accept them. Now He will remember their iniquity and punish their sins: They will return to Egypt. (8:13).
Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces; Judah has multiplied its fortified cities. But I will send fire upon their cities, and it will consume their citadels. (8:14).
crossRefs: Exodus 32:1-6: Aaron melts the people's gold earrings into a calf and they say these are your gods who brought you out of Egypt.
1 Kings 12:28-33: Jeroboam sets a golden calf in Bethel and one in Dan, appoints non-Levite priests, and invents his own feast.
Deuteronomy 28:49: The LORD will bring a nation from the ends of the earth to swoop down like an eagle.
Deuteronomy 17:16: The king is forbidden to send the people back to Egypt, the road Israel takes here.
Galatians 6:7-8: God is not mocked, and whatever a man sows he will reap in return.

translationNotes.note: 8:1 is an alarm. The shophar is a ram's horn, and a blast from it off the walls meant an enemy was in sight; Amos 3:6 and Jeremiah 6:1 both use it that way. Nesher covers eagle and griffon vulture, and the bird circling over the house of the LORD here is the second: a scavenger already overhead, waiting.

When the kingdom split, Jeroboam made two golden calves and set one at Bethel and one at Dan so his people would stop going up to Jerusalem to sacrifice (1 Kings 12:26-30). The bull was the standard image of the Canaanite storm god, who was shown as a bull or standing on one, so the object carried its meaning without a word spoken. 8:6 says the flat fact about it: a craftsman made it, and it is not God.

translationNotes.term: Sow the wind, reap the whirlwind
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רוּחַ יִזְרָעוּ וְסוּפָתָה יִקְצֹרוּ (ruach yizra'u ve-suphathah yiqtsoru)
translationNotes.note: Seed was broadcast by hand from a shoulder bag, so sowing wind is a man walking a field throwing nothing. The second half of 8:7 finishes the picture in farming terms: the standing stalk has no head on it, and if it somehow did, foreigners would eat it. Suphah is the desert whirlwind, the storm that strips a threshing floor bare.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִתְנוּ אֲהָבִים (hithnu ahavim, they have hired lovers)
translationNotes.note: 8:9-10 describes tribute. Menahem king of Israel paid Tiglath-pileser of Assyria a thousand talents of silver and raised it by assessing fifty shekels from every man of means (2 Kings 15:19-20). A talent is three thousand shekels, so that levy fell on about sixty thousand men. Hosea calls the payment what it is: money handed over to buy affection, which is the reverse of how a prostitute is normally paid.

translationNotes.term: A wild donkey off on its own
translationNotes.note: The pere is the onager, the wild ass of the eastern deserts, and Job 39:5-8 describes it as an animal that refuses a driver and ranges the salt flats alone. It does not join a herd and it cannot be worked. 8:9 says Ephraim went up to Assyria like one of those, and the point is that it went alone and by choice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִרְבָּה אֶפְרַיִם מִזְבְּחוֹת (hirbah Ephraim mizbechoth)
translationNotes.note: The law puts sacrifice in one place that God chooses and nowhere else (Deuteronomy 12:5-14). So altars stacking up is not extra devotion; it is the specific violation, and 8:11 says the altars themselves became altars for sinning. 8:12 adds the sharper charge, that the written instruction was treated as something foreign.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵמָּה מִצְרַיִם יָשׁוּבוּ (hemmah Mitsrayim yashuvu)
translationNotes.note: 8:13 sends Israel back where the nation started, which undoes the exodus as a sentence. Deuteronomy 28:68 had already put that threat in the covenant curses, a return to Egypt by ship. 9:3 sets the other destination beside it, Assyria, and the two together are the shape of the exile Hosea is announcing.

stories.keyTakeaway: God declares that Israel has broken his covenant and rejected him despite their claims of loyalty, condemning their self-made kings, idols, and false worship; they will face destruction and oppression because they sowed rebellion and will reap judgment.

stories.title: 🌪️ Hosea 9
summaryBullets: Do not rejoice, O Israel, with exultation like the nations, for you have played the harlot against your God; you have made love for hire on every threshing floor. (9:1).
The threshing floor and winepress will not feed them, and the new wine will fail them. (9:2).
They will not remain in the land of the LORD; Ephraim will return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria. (9:3).

They will not pour out wine offerings to the LORD, and their sacrifices will not please Him, but will be to them like the bread of mourners; all who eat will be defiled. For their bread will be for themselves; it will not enter the house of the LORD. (9:4).
What will you do on the appointed day, on the day of the LORD’s feast? (9:5).
For even if they flee destruction, Egypt will gather them and Memphis will bury them. Their precious silver will be taken over by thistles, and thorns will overrun their tents. (9:6).

The days of punishment have come; the days of retribution have arrived — let Israel know it. The prophet is called a fool, and the inspired man insane, because of the greatness of your iniquity and hostility. (9:7).
The prophet is Ephraim’s watchman, along with my God, yet the snare of the fowler lies on all his paths. Hostility is in the house of his God! (9:8).
They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah; He will remember their guilt; He will punish their sins. (9:9).

I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the firstfruits of the fig tree in its first season. But they went to Baal-peor, and consecrated themselves to Shame; so they became as detestable as the thing they loved. (9:10).
Ephraim’s glory will fly away like a bird, with no birth, no pregnancy, and no conception. (9:11).
Even if they raise their children, I will bereave them of each one. Yes, woe be to them when I turn away from them! (9:12).
I have seen Ephraim, like Tyre, planted in a meadow. But Ephraim will bring out his children for slaughter. (9:13).
Give them, O LORD— what will You give? Give them wombs that miscarry and breasts that dry up! (9:14).
All their evil appears at Gilgal, for there I hated them. I will drive them from My house for the wickedness of their deeds. I will no longer love them; all their leaders are rebellious. (9:15).
Ephraim is struck down; their root is withered; they cannot bear fruit. Even if they bear children, I will slay the darlings of their wombs. (9:16).
My God will reject them because they have not obeyed Him; and they shall be wanderers among the nations. (9:17).
crossRefs: Ruth 3:2-7: Boaz winnows barley on the threshing floor and sleeps beside the grain heap at harvest.
Numbers 25:1-9: Israel yokes itself to Baal of Peor at Shittim and twenty-four thousand die in the plague.
Judges 19:29-30: The outrage at Gibeah, the body cut in twelve pieces and sent through all Israel.
Deuteronomy 26:14: The worshiper swears he has not eaten the sacred portion while in mourning or while unclean.
Ezekiel 4:13: This is how the Israelites will eat defiled bread among the nations where I banish them.

translationNotes.term: A prostitute's wages on every threshing floor
translationNotes.note: A threshing floor was a levelled circle of rock or beaten earth on a windy rise outside town where oxen dragged a sledge over the cut grain and the chaff blew off. It was also the natural open ground for the harvest festival, and it doubled as public space (Ruth 3, 2 Samuel 24:18). Ethnan is the specific word for a harlot's fee. 9:1 says the harvest party on those floors has become payment taken from another god, and 9:2 answers that neither floor nor winepress will feed them.

9:3 says they will eat unclean food in Assyria, and the problem is not only the meat. Outside the land there was no altar, so no animal could be killed as an offering and no firstfruits given, and every meal fell outside the system Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 set up. Living in exile meant the whole diet was defiled by where it was eaten.

A corpse in a house made the house and everything open in it unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:14-15). Food from a house in mourning could not be brought to the altar, and Deuteronomy 26:14 has the worshipper swear he has not eaten the tithe while mourning. 9:4 says all their bread will be that bread: they will still eat, and none of it can be offered.

Memphis was the ancient capital of Lower Egypt, on the west bank of the Nile about fifteen miles south of modern Cairo, with the enormous burial ground of Saqqara beside it. 9:6 says Egypt will gather them and Memphis bury them. Being buried away from the family tomb was a real dread in Israel: Jacob made Joseph swear to carry his body home (Genesis 47:29-30), and Joseph made the same demand about his own bones (Genesis 50:25).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צֹפֶה (tsopheh, watchman) - פַּח יָקוֹשׁ (pach yaqosh, a fowler's trap)
translationNotes.note: A tsopheh stood on the wall or a tower to see trouble coming and sound it, and Ezekiel 33:1-7 spells out that a watchman who fails to warn carries the blood. 9:8 gives the prophet that post and then says a trap is laid on every road he walks. The pach is the spring trap a bird catcher hid under scattered grain.

Hosea names Gibeah twice, at 9:9 and 10:9, and expects the reader to know the story. Judges 19-20: men of Gibeah in Benjamin abused a Levite's concubine through the night until she died on the doorstep, the tribes went to war over it, and Benjamin was almost wiped out. It is the darkest episode in the book of Judges, and Hosea uses it as the floor Israel has now reached again.

Peor is a height in Moab, and 9:10 points at Numbers 25:1-9. Camped at Shittim, Israelite men went with Moabite women to the sacrifices of their gods, ate the offerings, bowed to them and yoked themselves to Baal of Peor; twenty-four thousand died in the plague that followed. Hosea puts that first act of joining a foreign cult at the head of the record, the moment the marriage broke.

Gilgal was the first camp west of the Jordan, where Joshua set up the twelve stones taken from the riverbed, circumcised the nation and kept the first Passover in the land (Joshua 4:19-5:12). By Hosea's day it was a working shrine, and he and Amos both name it as a place to stop going to (Hosea 4:15, Amos 4:4, Amos 5:5). 9:15 says all their evil is there.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel is warned not to celebrate like other nations because their unfaithfulness has invited punishment; crops will fail, they will be exiled to Egypt and Assyria, and God will make them barren and bereave them of their children.

stories.title: 🌾 Hosea 10
summaryBullets: Israel was a luxuriant vine, yielding fruit for himself. The more his fruit increased, the more he increased the altars. The better his land produced, the better he made the sacred pillars. (10:1).
Their hearts are devious; now they must bear their guilt. The LORD will break down their altars and demolish their sacred pillars. (10:2).
Surely now they will say, “We have no king, for we do not revere the LORD. What can a king do for us?” (10:3).
They speak mere words; with false oaths they make covenants. So judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of a field. (10:4).

The people of Samaria will fear for the calf of Beth-aven. Indeed, its people will mourn over it with its idolatrous priests — those who rejoiced in its glory — for it has been taken from them into exile. (10:5).
Yes, it will be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king. Ephraim will be seized with shame; Israel will be ashamed of its wooden idols. (10:6).
Samaria will be carried off with her king like a twig on the surface of the water. (10:7).

The high places of Aven will be destroyed— it is the sin of Israel; thorns and thistles will overgrow their altars. Then they will say to the mountains, “Cover us!” and to the hills, “Fall on us!” (10:8).
Since the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel, and there you have remained. Did not the battle in Gibeah overtake the sons of iniquity? (10:9).
I will chasten them when I please; nations will be gathered against them to put them in bondage for their double transgression. (10:10).
Ephraim is a well-trained heifer that loves to thresh; but I will place a yoke on her fair neck. I will harness Ephraim, Judah will plow, and Jacob will break the hard ground. (10:11).

Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion; break up your unplowed ground. For it is time to seek the LORD until He comes and sends righteousness upon you like rain. (10:12).
You have plowed wickedness and reaped injustice; you have eaten the fruit of lies. Because you have trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your mighty men, (10:13).

the roar of battle will rise against your people, so that all your fortresses will be demolished as Shalman devastated Beth-arbel in the day of battle, when mothers were dashed to pieces along with their children. (10:14).
Thus it will be done to you, O Bethel, because of your great wickedness. When the day dawns, the king of Israel will be utterly cut off. (10:15).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 4:3: “Break up fallow ground.”
Luke 23:30; Revelation 6:16: “Cover us” language echoed later.
2 Kings 17:5-6: Fall of Samaria to Assyria.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית־אָוֶן (‘house of wickedness’) vs. בֵּית־אֵל (‘house of God’), Greek (LXX): Βαιθὰν / Βαιθήλ, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): בית און / בית אל
translationNotes.note: Prophetic nickname mocking Bethel’s idol center (10:5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִיר נִירוּ לָכֶם, Greek (LXX): ἀροτριᾶτε ἑαυτοῖς χέρσον, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): חרושו לנא מתרבּא
translationNotes.note: Image for repentance: turn hard, untilled heart-soil (10:12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁלְמָן / בֵּית אַרְבְּאֵל, Greek (LXX): Σαλμανὰ / Βαιθαραβήλ, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): שלמנא / בית ערבאל
translationNotes.note: Likely an Assyrian ruler (e.g., Shalmaneser) and a town; the verse states mothers and children were smashed in that battle (10:14).

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

stories.keyTakeaway: Idol altars multiply as the heart twists; God calls for plowing a new heart-soil, but war comes, the king falls, and families are killed in siege.

stories.title: 🧒 Hosea 11
summaryBullets: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son. (11:1).
But the more I called Israel, the farther they departed from Me. They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images. (11:2).
It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by the arms, but they never realized that it was I who healed them. (11:3).
I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of love; I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them. (11:4).
Will they not return to the land of Egypt and be ruled by Assyria because they refused to repent? (11:5).
A sword will flash through their cities; it will destroy the bars of their gates and consume them in their own plans. (11:6).
My people are bent on turning from Me. Though they call to the Most High, He will by no means exalt them. (11:7).

How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel? How could I make you like Admah? How could I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred! (11:8).
I will not execute the full fury of My anger; I will not destroy Ephraim again. For I am God and not man — the Holy One among you — and I will not come in wrath. (11:9).
They will walk after the LORD; He will roar like a lion. When He roars, His children will come trembling from the west. (11:10).
They will come trembling like birds from Egypt and like doves from the land of Assyria. Then I will settle them in their homes, declares the LORD. (11:11).
Ephraim surrounds Me with lies, the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One. (11:12).
crossRefs: Matthew 2:15: Later citation of “Out of Egypt I called my son.”
Deuteronomy 32:10-12: God carrying His people.
Amos 1:8; Deuteronomy 29:23: Admah and Zeboiim named among ruined cities.

translationNotes.term: Out of Egypt I called my son
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִמִּצְרַיִם קָרָאתִי לִבְנִי, Greek (LXX): ἐξ Αἰγύπτου μετεκάλεσα τὰ τέκνα αὐτοῦ, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): מן מצרים קריתי לברִי
translationNotes.note: Hosea refers to Israel as God’s ‘son’ in the exodus. Later applied typologically in another context (Matt 2:15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew/English versification difference: Eng 11:12 = Heb 12:1; Greek/Aramaic follow Hebrew order
translationNotes.note: Be aware that some editions count 11:12 as 12:1 affecting cross-references into ch. 12.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִשְׁאַג, Greek (LXX): ὠρυήσεται, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): ישאג
translationNotes.note: Signal of God’s powerful call that draws scattered children back (11:10).

stories.keyTakeaway: God recalls loving and raising Israel, condemns their idol pull, announces Assyrian rule, yet restrains total destruction and promises a return at His lion-like call.

headings.text: Out of Egypt I Called My Son

stories.title: 🧩 Hosea 12
summaryBullets: Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind all day long; he multiplies lies and violence; he makes a covenant with Assyria and sends olive oil to Egypt. (12:1).
The LORD has a charge to bring against Judah. He will punish Jacob according to his ways and repay him according to his deeds. (12:2).
In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel, and in his vigor he wrestled with God. (12:3).
Yes, he struggled with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought His favor; he found Him at Bethel and spoke with Him there — (12:4).
the LORD God of Hosts, the LORD is His name of renown. (12:5).
But you must return to your God; maintain love and justice, and always wait on your God. (12:6).
A merchant loves to defraud with dishonest scales in his hands. (12:7).
And Ephraim boasts: “How rich I have become! I have found wealth for myself. In all my labors, they can find in me no iniquity that is sinful.” (12:8).
But I am the LORD your God ever since the land of Egypt. I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast. (12:9).
I spoke through the prophets and multiplied their visions; I gave parables through the prophets. (12:10).
Is there iniquity in Gilead? They will surely come to nothing. Do they sacrifice bulls in Gilgal? Indeed, their altars will be heaps of stones in the furrows of the field. (12:11).
Jacob fled to the land of Aram and Israel worked for a wife — for a wife he tended sheep. (12:12).
But by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved. (12:13).
Ephraim has provoked bitter anger, so his Lord will leave his bloodguilt upon him and repay him for his contempt. (12:14).
crossRefs: Genesis 25:26; Genesis 32:24-30: Jacob grasping the heel and wrestling.
Amos 8:5: False balances condemned.
Exodus 12-14; Numbers 12:6-8: Exodus and prophetic mediation.

translationNotes.term: He strove with God / with the angel
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׂרָה אֶת־אֱלֹהִים… שָׂרָה אֶל־מַלְאָךְ, Greek (LXX): ἠνίστατο πρὸς θεόν… ἐνίσχυσεν μετὰ ἀγγέλου, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): אתגבר עם קדם יי… עם מלאכא
translationNotes.note: Hosea narrates both ‘with God’ and ‘with the angel,’ echoing Genesis’ encounter where God’s messenger represents God’s presence.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּנַעַן (kenaʿan), Greek (LXX): Χαναάν, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): כנען
translationNotes.note: Wordplay: ‘merchant’ can read ‘Canaanite,’ hinting that Israel behaves like those famed for trade and deceit (12:7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וּבְנָבִיא הֶעֱלָה יְהוָה… וּבְנָבִיא נִשְׁמָר, Greek (LXX): διὰ προφήτου… διετηρήθη, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): בנביא אסתלק… ובנביא אתנטר
translationNotes.note: Affirms God’s use of a prophet (Moses) to bring up and watch over Israel (12:13).

stories.keyTakeaway: Hosea retells Jacob’s striving to urge repentance, exposes fraud and trust in wealth, and stresses that God speaks and saves through His prophets.

headings.text: A Reproof of Ephraim, Judah, and Jacob

stories.title: 🔥 Hosea 13
summaryBullets: When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel. But he incurred guilt through Baal, and he died. (13:1).

Now they sin more and more and make for themselves cast images, idols skillfully made from their silver, all of them the work of craftsmen. People say of them, “They offer human sacrifice and kiss the calves!” (13:2).
Therefore they will be like the morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes, like chaff blown from a threshing floor, like smoke through an open window. (13:3).
Yet I am the LORD your God ever since the land of Egypt; you know no God but Me, for there is no Savior besides Me. (13:4).
I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought. (13:5).
When they had pasture, they became satisfied; when they were satisfied, their hearts became proud, and as a result they forgot Me. (13:6).
So like a lion I will pounce on them; like a leopard I will lurk by the path. (13:7).
Like a bear robbed of her cubs I will attack them, and I will tear open their chests. There I will devour them like a lion, like a wild beast tearing them apart. (13:8).
You are destroyed, O Israel, because you are against Me — against your helper. (13:9).
Where is your king now to save you in all your cities, and the rulers to whom you said, “Give me a king and princes”? (13:10).
So in My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away. (13:11).
The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is stored up. (13:12).
Labor pains come upon him, but he is an unwise son. When the time arrives, he fails to present himself at the opening of the womb. (13:13).
I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death. Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting? Compassion is hidden from My eyes. (13:14).

Although he flourishes among his brothers, an east wind will come — a wind from the LORD rising up from the desert. His fountain will fail, and his spring will run dry. The wind will plunder his treasury of every precious article. (13:15).
Samaria will bear her guilt because she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword; their little ones will be dashed to pieces, and their pregnant women ripped open. (13:16).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 8:7: “They have rejected me from being king over them.”
2 Kings 17:5-6: Fall of Samaria to Assyria.
1 Corinthians 15:55: Later echoes of death/Sheol wording (text traditions vary).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִשְׁקוּ הָעֲגָלִים, Greek (LXX): καταφιλήσωσι τοὺς μόσχους, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): נשקין לעגליא
translationNotes.note: Act of reverence to calf-idols (13:2).

translationNotes.term: “I shall ransom…? / I will ransom…” (two readings)
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִיַּד שְׁאוֹל אֶפְדֵּם מִמָּוֶת אֶגְאָלֵם… אֱהִי דְבָרֶיךָ מָוֶת (interrogatives possible), Greek (LXX): ποῦ ἡ δίκη σου, θάνατε; ποῦ τὸ κέντρον σου, ᾅδη; Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): מן יד שאול אפדנם… היכן דינך מות
translationNotes.note: Hebrew can be read as questions (“Shall I ransom…? Where are your plagues, Death?”) or as promises/taunts. Later quotations follow Greek-style taunt (13:14).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָרִיּוֹת יְבֻקָּעוּ, Greek (LXX): διαρραγήσονται αἱ ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσαι, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): יתבקעון מעוברן
translationNotes.note: Describes atrocities in the fall of Samaria; historical reality of ancient siege warfare (13:16).

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

stories.keyTakeaway: Idols replace God and bring ruin. God questions their king-making, speaks of death and Sheol, and announces a brutal fall on Samaria.

stories.title: 🌿 Hosea 14
summaryBullets: Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled by your iniquity. (14:1).
Bring your confessions and return to the LORD. Say to Him: “Take away all our iniquity and receive us graciously, that we may present the fruit of our lips. (14:2).
Assyria will not save us, nor will we ride on horses. We will never again say, ‘Our gods!’ to the work of our own hands. For in You the fatherless find compassion.” (14:3).
I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them, for My anger has turned away from them. (14:4).
I will be like the dew to Israel; he will blossom like the lily and take root like the cedars of Lebanon. (14:5).
His shoots will sprout, and his splendor will be like the olive tree, his fragrance like the cedars of Lebanon. (14:6).
They will return and dwell in his shade; they will grow grain and blossom like the vine. His renown will be like the wine of Lebanon. (14:7).
O Ephraim, what have I to do anymore with idols? It is I who answer and watch over him. I am like a flourishing cypress; your fruit comes from Me. (14:8).

Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them. For the ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them but the rebellious stumble in them. (14:9).
crossRefs: Hebrews 13:15: “Fruit of lips” as praise (phrase echo).
Deuteronomy 33:13-16: Dew, fruitfulness blessings.
Psalm 1:3: Tree planted by streams; fruit imagery.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְשַׁלֵּם פָּרִים שְׂפָתֵינוּ, Greek (LXX): ἀποδώσομεν καρπὸν χειλέων ἡμῶν, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): נשלם תושבחת שפתין
translationNotes.note: Hebrew ‘parim’ can mean ‘bulls’ (sacrifices) or by wordplay ‘fruit’; sense: spoken offerings of repentance/praise (14:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשּׁוּר לֹא יוֹשִׁיעֵנוּ, Greek (LXX): Ἀσσὺρ οὐ μὴ σῴσῃ ἡμᾶς, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): אשור לא יפרקן
translationNotes.note: Turning from political/military dependence to reliance on God (14:3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶהְיֶה כַטָּל, Greek (LXX): ἔσομαι ὡς δρόσος, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): אהיה כטל
translationNotes.note: Quiet, life-giving refreshment in a dry land (14:5).

stories.keyTakeaway: A final call to return with honest words and to drop idols and foreign saviors. God promises healing, steady love, and fresh growth like dew on a renewed land.

intro:
Hosea was written by Hosea son of Beeri (Hosea 1:1), the prophet of the northern kingdom of Israel during its final decades. His ministry spanned roughly forty years, from the latter part of the reign of Jeroboam II of Israel (793-753 BC) through the reigns of the Judahite kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Hosea 1:1), placing the composition of the book between approximately 755 BC and 715 BC. Hosea was a native of the northern kingdom of Israel, the only writing prophet who ministered in the north and was himself a northerner (Amos also ministered in the north but was a Judahite from Tekoa, Amos 1:1). Nothing is known of his father Beeri outside Hosea 1:1. God commanded Hosea to marry Gomer daughter of Diblaim (Hosea 1:3), and she bore him three children whose names were prophetic signs: Jezreel (Hosea 1:4, named for the valley where Jehu massacred the house of Ahab), Lo-Ruhamah ("Not Loved," Hosea 1:6), and Lo-Ammi ("Not My People," Hosea 1:9). Gomer proved unfaithful, and Hosea 3:1 records God commanding the prophet to take her back at a later point. The prophet's name Hoshea (הוֹשֵׁעַ, "salvation") is shared with Joshua son of Nun (whose original name before Moses changed it was also Hoshea, Numbers 13:8, 13:16) and with Hoshea son of Elah, the last king of the northern kingdom (732-722 BC, 2 Kings 17); all three are distinct figures with the same Hebrew name.

The historical setting is the final decades of the northern kingdom of Israel before its destruction by Assyria. Jeroboam II's long and prosperous reign (793-753 BC) had brought the northern kingdom to its greatest territorial extent since Solomon, but his death triggered political chaos. The next thirty years saw six kings: Zechariah (753-752 BC, assassinated after six months), Shallum (752 BC, assassinated after one month), Menahem (752-742 BC, who paid tribute to the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III), Pekahiah (742-740 BC, assassinated), Pekah (740-732 BC, assassinated), and Hoshea son of Elah (732-722 BC, the last king of Israel, who was deposed and imprisoned by Shalmaneser V of Assyria). The Neo-Assyrian Empire under Tiglath-Pileser III (745-727 BC), Shalmaneser V (727-722 BC), and Sargon II (722-705 BC) repeatedly campaigned through the Levant, demanding tribute and finally destroying Samaria in 722 BC and deporting the ten northern tribes. Hosea ministered through this entire collapse alongside his contemporary Amos (also in the north) and Isaiah and Micah (in Judah to the south). Egypt under the 25th Dynasty (the Kushite or Ethiopian Pharaohs) offered a tempting but unreliable alliance against Assyria; Israel's foreign-policy oscillation between Egypt and Assyria forms much of Hosea's political background.

Hosea is the twenty-eighth book of the Christian Old Testament and the first of the twelve Minor Prophets (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi). In the Hebrew Bible the twelve are counted as a single book called Trei Asar (Aramaic for "the Twelve"), preserved as a single scroll within the Latter Prophets. The Hebrew name Hoshea (הוֹשֵׁעַ) means "salvation" or "he saves," from the verbal root yasha ("to save," the same root as Yeshua/Jesus). Hebrew manuscript fragments of Hosea were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; the earliest copies (4Q76 and others) date to the 2nd century BC.
